title: An arrow resting on truth
hookLine: an uncle and a nephew face each other at the fire, and Lakshmana makes a vow on his brother's name

cards: The grove at Nikumbhila is dark with trees, and somewhere inside, a fire is burning.
Lakshmana's army crashes into the rakshasas guarding it, and the fighting gets so loud and close that Indrajit has to leave his offering unfinished and come out. He climbs into his chariot.
And the first face he sees in the enemy line isn't Lakshmana's. It's his uncle's: Vibhishana, who knew about the fire, the grove and the secret condition, and brought them here.

teach.b: Indrajit's words are bitter. You were born here, he says, you're my father's brother, and you've brought the enemy to your own nephew. Vibhishana answers without shouting.
I was born among the rakshasas, but my nature isn't cruel. I left my brother because of what he was doing: carrying off another man's wife, harming those who had done him no wrong.
Then the duel begins, Lakshmana and Indrajit, long and close: chariots wrecked, armor split, both men bleeding.
At last Lakshmana fits the weapon of Indra, king of the gods, to his bow, and before he lets it go, he speaks a vow.

If Rama, son of Dasharatha, is righteous, true to his word and unmatched in courage, then let this arrow kill Ravana's son. The arrow flies, and Indrajit falls. Lakshmana doesn't rest the arrow on his own strength.
He rests it on his brother's truth.
Scholars call this kind of vow an act of truth: if what I say is true, let it happen. Behind it sits one of Hinduism's oldest convictions: truth, satya, isn't only not lying.
It's a power that holds the world up, and in the end it wins.
The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words: satyameva jayate, truth alone triumphs. India took them as its national motto. In Lanka, Ravana hears and loses his mind with grief.
He rushes toward the ashoka grove to kill Sita.
A minister named Suparshva steps in front of him. You, a learned king, would kill a woman? Fight Rama instead.

how: Lakshmana's vow before the final arrow, resting on Rama's righteousness and truth, is often quoted by Ramayana teachers. Satyameva jayate, from the Mundaka Upanishad, is India's national motto, written beneath its state emblem.

games.q: you're Lakshmana. the duel has gone on and on, and you're both wounded. you take up Indra's weapon. what do you do before you shoot?
o: speak a vow on Rama's goodness.
offer Indrajit one last chance to surrender.
games.why: he vows: if Rama is righteous, true and unmatched in courage, let this arrow kill Ravana's son. truth, not strength, carries the arrow.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you know is true and good: a promise you've kept, a person who has never lied to you. For a few slow breaths, let what you're facing rest on that, the way Lakshmana rested his arrow on Rama's truth.
If you pray, say it softly three times: satyameva jayate. If you don't, say: truth alone wins.

wordCard.voice: Indrajit's death. At Nikumbhila, his rite broken, he falls to Lakshmana's arrow of Indra, shot on a vow resting on Rama's truth.

orig.note: Sanskrit satyam eva jayate: truth alone triumphs, from the Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.6); India's national motto.

carryVoice: Your line: satyameva jayate, truth alone wins. With his son gone, Ravana has no one left to send. Until tomorrow.
